I

Industry & analogy

Who is moving on the grid, who is stacking capacity — and why the forms still miss the peril.

The connections clearing fastest are non-firm — interruptible by contract. The market prices damage; the peril is availability.

Why now

Britain is connecting tens of gigawatts of data-centre and energy load to a grid that can no longer promise to keep it switched on. Compute is a 24/7, always-on consumer that monetises every hour — so for the first time the demand side is paying a premium for firmness itself, and the data-centre build-out has put that load at the front of a queue the network cannot firmly serve.1,2 Non-firm risk is not an old peril rediscovered; it is a new one, created by the collision of an always-on demand curve with an interruptible grid.

Parallel markets

Grid reform runs ahead of wording reform

The grid side is not waiting. A 2025 synthesis of global non-firm access identifies four dominant models — capacity-limited, time-limited, dynamic operating envelopes, and fully flexible active network management — now written into law or code from Great Britain through Spain, Germany, Belgium, and Australia.3,4 Britain's Flexible Plug and Play pilots cut connection cost by up to 87% and lead times by 57% by accepting curtailable access instead of reinforcement; Ofgem's Access SCR then standardised that trade for larger users, with curtailment limits and end-dates in the connection offer the loss adjuster can read but the BI wording cannot trigger on.3,4 The EU's 2024 electricity-market directive now requires Member States to offer flexible connections where capacity is scarce — interruptibility is becoming a register fact, not a negotiated footnote.5,3

The insurance side is moving on a parallel track, but toward capacity not trigger fit. In roughly eighteen months the London and Bermuda markets have stacked specialist facilities — Marsh's $2.7bn Nimbus programme, Aon's $3.5bn data-centre lifecycle facility, parametric SLA mirrors from Lloyd's coverholders — while S&P Global sizes a ~$10bn premium runway for hyperscale campuses and Swiss Re warns of a ~$10bn single nat-cat tail on a US data centre.6,7,8,9,10 Almost all of it still routes through all-risks physical-damage and time-element wordings; the curtailment-predictability spectrum the grid regulators now encode has no mirror in the binder.11,3

The incumbents

Why the energy market hasn't priced it

There is no shortage of energy-insurance capacity in London. Dozens of carriers, Lloyd's syndicates, MGAs and brokers write power, renewables and construction risk every day. So why does an unpriced peril survive inside a sophisticated market? Three structural reasons, none of them stupidity. First, the form is sticky: energy cover is sold on all-risks physical-damage-and-time-element wordings refined over decades, and a curtailment generates no damage event for a loss adjuster to find.11 Second, the incentives point sideways: an underwriter is rewarded for growing premium on a familiar form, not for inventing an availability product whose loss history does not yet exist. Third, the peril is new: the always-on compute load that makes firmness valuable is a phenomenon of the last few years, and rates lag exposure by exactly the interval it takes a loss to show up in the triangles.

The specialist market is racing to add limit, not fit: broker facilities quote billions in aggregate data-centre capacity, carrier research sizes double-digit premium runways, and parametric SLA products exist in fragments — but the connection agreement's curtailment cap, end-date, and predictability class rarely appear in the schedule.6,7,8,10 Curtailment cost is already observable in the system operator's constraint-cost data12 — yet almost none of it flows into an energy premium. That gap between an observable, rising cost and a flat rate is the definition of mispricing.

Same peril, four layers of the chain — each carrying it in a different form.
II

The landscape

Map the field before you score it — who sits where in the value chain, and how the population spreads on two axes.

The value chain

Four layers, one risk

The same peril sits differently at each link of the chain, and preparedness at one layer does not imply it at the next. A carrier can be capital-strong while the MGA binding its energy facility has no availability wording; a colocation asset can be heavily exposed while the reinsurer behind the cedant models only physical cat.

L1
Carriers & Lloyd's syndicates
Hold the balance sheet. Exposure is the concentration of energy / data-centre / specialty premium in the book; preparedness is capital strength, availability products, and the expertise to price curtailment rather than damage.
Composite insurers, London-market specialty carriers, Lloyd's syndicates
L2
MGAs & brokers
Price and place without (mostly) carrying the balance sheet. Exposure is the risk routed through their facilities and binders; preparedness is the products they can actually structure and the talent to broke an availability tower.
Delegated-authority MGAs, wholesale and London-chain brokers
L3
Energy & data-centre assets
Originate the peril. Exposure is the share of capacity on flexible / non-firm connections and queue position; preparedness is backup generation, monitoring, and how firmly the connection is secured.
Hyperscale & colocation campuses, batteries, generation behind a non-firm connection
L4
Reinsurers & capacity
Stand behind the carriers. Exposure is correlated tail risk aggregated across cedants on the same constrained network; preparedness is rated capital and the modelling to see the correlation the primary market misses.
Property-cat and specialty reinsurers, retrocession capacity

III

Mechanics

How the peril works, how the score works — briefly, before the full case.

The frame

Exposure against Preparedness

Every entity is placed on two scored axes. Exposure measures the size of the bet: how much non-firm, curtailable load sits in the book or the asset, how concentrated it is on the same grid geography, and how badly today's wordings miss the peril. Preparedness measures the ability to carry it: whether the underwriter has the data, the products, the modelling, the expertise and the capital to actually hold the risk it has written.

Margin of Safety = Preparedness − Exposure. Not who is exposed? — who is exposed beyond their ability to carry it?

How interruption works

Why interruption is not damage

A non-firm connection fails in a way the market's instruments do not register. There is no broken asset, no proximate physical cause, no repair. The grid operator, acting entirely within its rights, instructs a curtailment; the facility loses availability; the penalty or the lost revenue lands. A business-interruption policy that triggers on physical damage to insured property11,13 never sees it.

Curtailment is a compound loss14 — frequency times severity — and both terms move with grid constraints and queue position, not with the asset's physical condition. Covering it means a trigger that pays on an index of interruption rather than a loss adjuster's finding of damage, with the basis risk15,16 that any parametric line inherits.

Why cat and cyber miss it

A catastrophe model needs a physical hazard footprint; curtailment has none — the hazard is in the connection agreement and the constraint map.17

Cyber underwriters learned to price a non-physical peril, but aggregation runs through shared software and service providers — not shared grid geography.18

Non-firm power risk correlates through the network: two data centres behind the same constraint boundary move together whether or not they share code.2 Any serious attempt to price it starts with registers that describe the grid, not an imported event set.

How we score

Every rating names its source class — register, filing, derived field, or sourced research — and links to the primary. Outside-in judgements fuse with register readings by published credibility rules;19 where registers are still landing, magnitudes stay directional until measured share clears the L5 threshold. Full scoring pipeline: methodology.

With the map and the mechanics set: three claims, one instrument.
IV

Argument & proposal

Substantiate the case, name the instrument, close on who can carry what the market has not yet priced.

The case

A peril the market was not built to see

For a century the large industrial insurance contract has answered a single question: what happens if the thing breaks? That question built the property and business-interruption market. It is also, increasingly, the wrong one for the fastest-growing concentration of insured value in Britain. The dominant risk to a data centre or a grid-scale energy asset is no longer that it breaks. It is that it is lawfully, contractually, and repeatedly switched off.20

This essay makes three claims and proposes one instrument. First, that non-firm power risk is large, growing, and structurally mispriced. Second, that the models the market reaches for cannot see it, for reasons that are architectural rather than incidental. Third, that pricing it correctly requires the two-axis construct above — exposure against preparedness — not a single hazard score. The instrument is an outside-in map of exactly that, reconciled from the registers and filings the placement chain already walks past.

The economics

Why the number is large

The data-centre build-out has put a demand queue measured in the tens of gigawatts in front of the system operator,21 and the connections clearing it are disproportionately the flexible, curtailable kind. A hyperscale facility contracts for tens to hundreds of megawatts and sells its tenants a four-nines availability SLA — roughly 52 minutes of permitted downtime a year. A sustained curtailment is a direct breach, and power is already the single largest cause of significant data-centre outages.20,1

The financial value at risk is contracted load times hours off times the penalty rate per hour. None of those terms appears in a physical-damage policy. The market is therefore carrying an exposure whose severity it does not compute and whose frequency it does not track. The premium that should attach to availability cover is a function the existing book never evaluates; the premium that does attach is zero, because the cover does not exist.

The market is not underpricing this peril. It is not pricing it at all.

The proposal

A wedge, not a data vendor

The cat-model instinct is to reduce a risk to a single number and rank the market by it. For this peril that instinct misranks the field. The same non-firm exposure is well-carried by an underwriter with the data, products, modelling and capital to hold it, and dangerous in the hands of one without. A one-axis score cannot express that, because it collapses the two things whose difference is the entire signal.

The index is a wedge: the proprietary, primary-source understanding of a peril the rest of the market underwrites blind. The measured features — connection-gate status, flexible-connection share, aggregation over shared grid geography, trigger gap against parametric availability — are built to be exactly the edge that lets you price the gap and carry it. Whoever holds that picture first is positioned not to sell a score, but to write the cover that does not yet exist.

The re-pricing

Rules that turn firmness into a fact

Connections reform is converting firmness into a dated, registered fact. As the queue moves to a gated model, an asset's firmness becomes an objective register entry: which gate it sits behind, on what terms, with what curtailment rights attached.22,21 Live rules such as CMP434/448 and GC0166 start re-pricing the same sub-factors on every renewal.

The opportunity

Whoever can measure it can carry it

Parametric availability, SLA mirrors, curtailment indices — the fragments exist. No one yet holds the full stack: measured non-firm exposure, basis-minimised trigger, aggregation-aware pricing, and rated paper in whitespace.

The market deploys capacity onto whoever looks exposed on a damage view, while genuine non-firm losses concentrate where exposure has outrun preparedness — and the genuinely capable sit in under-priced whitespace. The rankings and profiles below test whether that divergence shows up in the live data.

Findings

What the data shows

A model is only interesting if it sees something. The current index is a provisional slice of 115 entities across 4 layers (39 carriers, 35 MGAs/brokers, 24 assets, 17 tail), scored largely at the assessed tier while the live registers are loaded — so what follows is a read of structure, not a published ranking. Only 22% of the score yet rests on measured evidence. The point is not yet the magnitudes. It is that the shape the model was built to detect is already legible in the data.

26.3Median Margin of Safetyspread 126.3 pts tail-to-tail
The scatter is the argument made visible — each dot is one entity on axes the market does not yet publish together. Position is exposure against preparedness; the margin is their difference.

Three things stand out even on this slice. First, the field is not uniformly exposed: 24 entities (21%) sit in Earning it and 20 (17%) in Sidelined, with only 36 (31%) in the outright danger zone — Hiscox London Market, Kao Data — Harlow Campus, Aviva, Price Forbes (Ardonagh) and 32 others. That is exactly the pattern a damage-only view would miss, because it flags as fine an entity whose exposure to non-firm power is invisible to its own wordings.

Second, the spread between the most and least prepared is wide and interpretable. The largest positive Margin of Safety belongs to Swiss Re Corporate Solutions (Margin +63.7), whose preparedness — rated capital, named availability capability — runs well ahead of the exposure it has taken on. The most negative belongs to Gate Burton Energy Park — West Lindsey, Lincolnshire, England (Margin -62.6), an entity whose non-firm intensity sits ahead of any visible mitigation. The model is not asserting these are good or bad businesses; it is locating each on the one axis that matters for this peril — whether the bet is matched by the means to carry it.

Third, there is genuine whitespace: 35 entities including Beazley, AXA XL, Munich Re, Descartes Underwriting and 31 others sit in the capable-but-under-deployed quadrant. On the thesis of this index, that is where the unwritten availability cover should originate — underwriters with the capital and competence to carry the risk who are not yet earning on it.23

By layer

Where the signal concentrates

The peril does not distribute evenly across the value chain. Exposed concentrates in Layer 3 (assets) (20 of 36) — Gate Burton Energy Park — West Lindsey, Lincolnshire, England, Nscale — Loughton, Essex AI Data Centre, QTS / Blackstone Cambois (Blyth) AI Campus — Northumberland, Seagreen Offshore Wind Farm — Firth of Forth, off Angus, Scotland, Coalburn 1 BESS — South Lanarkshire, Scotland and 15 others among the asset names — which is structurally right: non-firm intensity is a register fact at Layer 3 before it propagates upward into carrier books. Carriers and MGAs show up more often in Whitespace (17 at Layer 1, 11 at Layer 2) and Sidelined than in Exposed, because preparedness inputs (capital, product fit, specialist teams) are easier to evidence at balance-sheet layers than curtailment exposure is to see from the outside.

Layer 1 still contributes 10 Exposed names — carriers whose book concentration and trigger gap outrun parametric or availability product fit. That is a different failure mode from the asset case: not “curtailed tomorrow” but “writing damage-only cover on a peril whose loss is lawful switch-off.”11,13

The exposed slice

Where exposure runs ahead of preparedness

Within Exposed, the deepest negative margin is Gate Burton Energy Park — West Lindsey, Lincolnshire, England (Margin -62.6). Of 24 scored assets, 13 have a firm Gate register status and 11 remain unknown pending a Gate-2 record — the index shows the number but does not infer firmness. The honest read is that the L3 Exposed cluster (20 of 36) is directionally right while magnitudes and ordering will move as NESO and DNO registers are fully ingested.22,24

The headline finding is not a ranking. It is that exposure and preparedness genuinely come apart — across 115 entities and 126.3 points of margin spread — which is the whole reason a one-axis hazard score would mislead, and a margin would not.

Reading it honestly

What would change, and what would not

Only 22% of the score yet rests on measured evidence, so the index is marked provisional and should be read as direction, not measurement. What moves as the live data lands is the magnitude and ordering within each quadrant: as non-firm intensity is pulled from the connection registers and capital from the filings, entities will shift across the median cut-lines (currently exp ≥ 53.8, prep ≥ 61.2) and the rank order will firm up. What does not change is the construct — the two axes, the margin, and the finding that they separate. This section re-runs automatically on every build, against whatever the registers then say.24,25

Objections

Isn't this just a climate or catastrophe peril?

No — the trigger is lawful switch-off under connection terms, not weather. Damage-BI and cat models price the wrong event; NFRI scores who carries interruptible-power exposure and who has the data, product and capital to underwrite it.

Why should I trust outside-in research scores?

Every sub-factor fuses register and filing evidence with research prior by credibility weight. Measured share and the L5 publication gate are printed on every build — PROVISIONAL until the blend clears 60%.

Does Margin of Safety replace underwriting judgment?

It compresses two axes the market does not publish together into one directional number. It is an index for discovery and relative placement — not an audited rating or investment advice.

In force

Rules that re-price firmness

doloop discipline: not what's proposed — what landed. Each modification flags records it re-scores when Gate or curtailment terms change.

Methodology

Two axes, fused from evidence

Every entity is scored on two axes — Exposure and Preparedness — each a weighted sum of five sub-factors on a 0–4 scale, rescaled to 0–100. The scoring is arithmetic in code, never a model's free-text opinion. The judgement enters only where a register cannot reach, and even there it is fused with whatever hard data exists, weighted by how much that data deserves to be trusted.

The axis score is E = (Σ wi · reff,i / 4) × 100: a weighted average of effective sub-factor ratings, where each reff is itself a fusion of a register reading and a research reading (below). Margin of Safety is simply Preparedness − Exposure, and the two median cut-lines define the four quadrants.

Fusion

Latent × deterministic

Each sub-factor can carry two ratings: a deterministic rating derived in code from a register or filing, and a latent rating from sourced research judgement. The effective rating is a credibility-weighted blend19 — reff = clamp[0,4]( λ·rdet + (1−λ)·rlat ) — where λ is set by the evidence tier of the deterministic input. Measured registers dominate; an assessed sub-factor falls back entirely to the research prior.

Credibility weight λ by evidence tier (lowered slightly when input confidence is medium / low)
Tier of deterministic inputλEffect
Measured (register)0.95Score is the register, essentially. Research prior barely moves it.
Derived (computed from registers)0.85Mostly the computed value; small room for judgement.
Disclosed (filing / rating)0.80Filing-led, judgement at the margin.
Assessed (no measurement)0.00Falls back entirely to the sourced research rating.

λ = max(0, λ_tier + δ_confidence), with δ = 0 / −0.05 / −0.10 for high / medium / low confidence in the deterministic input.

Evidence tiers

How directly each number is evidenced

Every value carries a tier, and the tier is load-bearing: it sets λ and it is shown on the entity drill-down. The four tiers describe how directly a rating is evidenced — from a register read straight off, to a research judgement made where no measurement reaches. A reader can follow any rating back to its source.

TierMeaningExample
MeasuredRead directly from a primary register.MW on a flexible connection in the DNO Embedded Capacity Register.
DisclosedStated in a filing, rating or regulatory record.Financial-strength rating; Solvency II SCR coverage.
DerivedComputed deterministically from measured / disclosed inputs.Herfindahl index over grid supply points.
AssessedSourced research judgement where no measurement exists.Pricing capability, capped and confidence-limited.

Reading it

Provisional, and open about it

Some sub-factors can be measured and others cannot: three Preparedness sub-factors — data & monitoring, underwriting expertise, pricing & modelling — rest on judgement by their nature, so the measurable load sits mostly on the Exposure axis, where non-firm intensity comes from the registers, book concentration from filings, and aggregation is derived from grid geography.

While the live registers and filings are still being read in across the universe, scores stay provisional until the publication gate clears — see the Methodology page for the measured-share threshold and current status. The direction of each score is defensible; magnitudes firm up as register tiers land. Open any entity for its own provenance trail.

From register to rating

Each sub-factor's path from source to 0–4 rating is fixed in the rubric, so the same inputs always produce the same score. The table below traces that path for each one: the data is collected first, and the rating follows from it.

Sub-factorTarget tierComputation
non_firm_intensitymeasured / derivedΣ(non-firm MW) / Σ(MW) from ECR flexible-connection flags or TEC gate status.
book_concentrationdisclosed / derivedShare of GWP / segmental revenue in energy + property + data-centre classes.
aggregation_correlationderivedHerfindahl index of covered MW across grid supply points / constraint boundaries.
trigger_gapdisclosed → assessedDoes relevant cover rely on damage triggers only? Evidenced by wordings; capped if press-only.
tenor_mismatchdisclosed → assessedMax cover tenor vs years of credible curtailment claims history.
capital_reinsurancedisclosed(rating, SCR coverage %) → 0–4 via fixed lookup.

    Sources

    References

    Every rating links to a primary source. The references cited across this index are listed below in citation order — academic, regulatory, actuarial and market sources, each with the role it plays in the model.

    1. 1
      International Energy Agency (IEA) (2024) Electricity 2024 — Analysis and forecast to 2026 (data-centre & AI electricity demand) Industry research
      Evidence that 24/7 AI/compute load is driving the demand surge and the value of firm, always-on power — the why-now behind non-firm risk.
    2. 2
      Mahuze, R.; Gressel, C.; Amadeh, A.; Zhang, K. M. (2026) The Potential Welfare Gains from Curtailment Trading Under Non-Firm Interconnection Academic
      Explicitly models data centres accepting curtailment risk via non-firm interconnection for faster grid access.; VOLL heterogeneity ($4k–$667k/MWh) means pro-rata curtailment destroys surplus — basis for trigger_gap / parametric design.; Curtailment Credit Market achieves 1.41–1.83× welfare vs pro-rata — quantifies inefficiency of blunt allocation rules.
    3. 3
      Monterde, R.; Alvarez, E. F.; Valarezo, O. (2025) Non-Firm Grid Connections: A Review of Access Types, Mechanisms, and Regulatory Frameworks Academic
      Four models: capacity-limited, time-limited, DOEs, fully flexible ANM; UK Flexible Plug and Play (87% cost / 57% lead-time); curtailment predictability spectrum → trigger_gap; LIFO/pro-rata → compound loss; reviews UK/ES/DE/BE/AU/EU/US frameworks.
    4. 4
      Ofgem (2022) Access and Forward-Looking Charges Significant Code Review — Final Decision Regulatory
      Mandates standardised non-firm (curtailable) connection option for larger DNO users from April 2023.; Requires explicit curtailment limits and end-dates in connection offers — measurable contract fields.; Defines interruptible access: network can curtail import/export; trade-off is faster/cheaper connection.
    5. 5
      European Parliament and Council (2024) Directive (EU) 2024/1711 — common rules for the internal market in electricity Regulatory
      Member States must support flexible/non-firm grid connections where capacity is scarce; EU-wide anchor cited in Monterde et al. 2025 review.
    6. 6
      Marsh (2026) Nimbus insurance facility for digital infrastructure Broker
      London Market facility capacity and specialty placement for data-centre construction/operational risk.
    7. 7
      Aon plc (2026) Data Center Lifecycle Insurance Program (DCLP) Broker
      $3.5bn CAR/DSU/PD/BI + cyber DSU; Lloyd's panel; risk engineering and cyber impact modelling.
    8. 8
      S&P Global Ratings (2026) Data Centers Offer A Hyperscale Pool Of Insurable Risks Industry research
      ~$2tn insurable base; PML/MFL layered limits not full TIV; ~$10bn premium runway; aggregation on multiphase campuses.
    9. 9
      Swiss Re Institute (2026) sigma insights 07/2026: Insuring AI — data centre value accumulation risks Carrier research
      Split-program opacity; nat-cat accumulation on DC; liquid cooling ~24% loss costs; premiums $10.6bn→$24.2bn by 2030.
    10. 10
      Parametrix (2025) SLA insurance for data centres MGA
      Lloyd's coverholder parametric SLA mirror; telemetry monitoring; trigger_gap=0 design; triple-net financing.
    11. 11
      Lloyd's Market Association (2023) Business Interruption and Non-Damage BI market guidance Market guidance
      Physical-damage trigger requirement in conventional BI vs non-damage extensions; trigger_gap framing.
    12. 12
      National Energy System Operator (NESO) (2025) Balancing / constraint costs (Monthly Balancing Services Summary & data portal) Primary data
      Curtailment / network-constraint cost as an observable proxy for non-firm interruption frequency and severity; supports the compound-loss view.
    13. 13
      Che-Castaldo, J. P.; Cousin, R.; Daryanto, S.; et al. (2021) Critical Risk Indicators (CRIs) for the electric power grid: a survey and discussion of interconnected effects Academic
      Multi-domain CRIs (climate, finance, hydrology, ecology, space weather) → grid interruption; SAIDI/SAIFI/reserve margin; Systemic Risk Indicators via VAR/Granger networks; power interruption as risk realisation; maps to register-based sub-factors and aggregation_correlation.
    14. 14
      Klugman, S. A.; Panjer, H. H.; Willmot, G. E. (2012) Loss Models: From Data to Decisions Textbook
      Compound loss E[L]=E[N]·E[S]; frequency-severity decomposition for curtailment/availability events.
    15. 15
      Maier, M. J.; Scherer, M. (2025) Expectiles as basis risk-optimal payment schemes in parametric insurance Academic
      Basis risk = payout vs true loss gap under index/parametric triggers; motivates trigger_gap sub-factor.
    16. 16
      Teh, T.-L.; Woolnough, C. (2019) A Better Trigger: Indices for Insurance Academic
      Separates upside basis risk q from downside basis risk r — higher correlation ≠ better index; Provides dominance ranking for binary and multivalue indices across heterogeneous buyers; Builds on Clarke (2016) viability condition for insurance purchase under basis risk
    17. 17
      Lloyd's (2024) Realistic Disaster Scenarios (RDS) — market-wide stress testing Market guidance
      Correlated tail scenarios across syndicate portfolios; aggregation_correlation and capital_reinsurance.
    18. 18
      Liu, M.; Huang, J.; Liu, S. (2026) Artificial intelligence assets and energy markets: Risk correlation dynamics and determinants Academic
      AI–clean energy mean DCC ~0.67; AI hedges gas/INE, diversifies WTI/Brent; CPU/DRV/EPU strengthen correlations; regional crude heterogeneity; maps to aggregation_correlation and RDS stress.
    19. 19
      Bühlmann, H.; Gisler, A. (2005) A Course in Credibility Theory and Its Applications Textbook
      Precision-weighted blend of experience (deterministic/register) and prior (latent/research) — theoretical basis for fusion λ.
    20. 20

      Extends Clarke four-state model with farmer-chosen trigger level k; Optimal triggers target catastrophic tails even if downside basis risk r(k) rises; Explains why low uptake may reflect premium design, not insurmountable basis risk

      SCR ratio thresholds for capital_reinsurance deterministic mapping.

    30. 30
      Descartes Underwriting (2025) Parametric product suite for data centres MGA

    31. 31
      Raj Kumari Bahl (2025) Determination of Premium for Insurance Policies covering Long Outages in Cloud Services under the Exponential-Pareto Model Academic
      Applies six standard actuarial premium principles (variance, Esscher, etc.) to SLA long-outage cover under Exponential-Pareto ON/OFF model (Naldi framework).; Long outages modelled as Poisson sum of Bernoulli indicators on outage duration threshold w — links SLA refund mechanics to claim frequency.; Explicitly motivated by CSP SLA refund obligations and insurer need to price tail long-outage risk without eroding capital.
